05 ADHD and sleep · class card

ADHD

attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) drugs · methylphenidate · dexmethylphenidate · amphetamine salts · dextroamphetamine · lisdexamfetamine · atomoxetine · guanfacine · clonidine

Key point
  • Stimulant: first from age 6
  • Behavioral therapy (parent training): first under 6
  • Cardiac history and exam: before a stimulant
  • Electrocardiogram (ECG): consider adding with known heart disease, a suggestive exam or a family history of sudden cardiac death
  • Atomoxetine: when misuse or diversion is a risk
  • Liver injury on atomoxetine: stop it for good
  • Mania on a stimulant: taper or stop the stimulant and treat the mania
  • Guanfacine and clonidine: taper; do not stop abruptly
Drugs

Methylphenidate Ritalin Concerta: stimulant

Dexmethylphenidate Focalin: one mirror-image form (enantiomer) of methylphenidate

Amphetamine salts Adderall; dextroamphetamine Dexedrine: stimulants

Lisdexamfetamine Vyvanse: a prodrug of dextroamphetamine

Atomoxetine Strattera: nonstimulant

Intuniv, clonidine: nonstimulant alpha-2 agonists Guanfacine formsExtended-release guanfacine is not swapped milligram for milligram with the immediate-release tablet The two forms are absorbed differently

Mechanism

Methylphenidate: dopamine and norepinephrine reuptake blocked more of both at the synapse

Amphetamines: catecholamines displaced from storage vesicles released into the synapse

Lisdexamfetamine: activated in the gut usable with a drug-misuse history

Atomoxetine: norepinephrine transporter blocked no action on the nucleus accumbens no addiction risk

Guanfacine, clonidine: alpha-2 agonists less presynaptic norepinephrine release hypotension, bradycardia, sleepiness

Uses

: stimulant from age 6; behavioral therapy first under 6 ADHD in preschool childrenBehavioral therapy comes firstMedication may be considered if the response is inadequate or symptoms are moderate to severe

Teenage girl once on methylphenidate, now questioning rules: schoolwork fine; no inattention, hyperactivity or impulsivity

Defiance: chosen, no impairment

Teenager with no ADHD symptoms: educate the parents about adolescent development and reassure them; no methylphenidate restart

Atomoxetine: when a stimulant is ruled out, as with a high risk of misuse or diversion

: when stimulants fail, in children and teens Alpha-2 agonists in ADHDGuanfacine: works better than clonidine for childhood ADHDGuanfacine and clonidine: less effective than stimulantsGuanfacine and clonidine: limited data in adults

Lisdexamfetamine: also binge eating disorder

Narcolepsy: methylphenidate or an amphetamine, second line after modafinil

Methylphenidate: also used in severe depression when life expectancy is short

Clonidine, guanfacine: also tics

Adverse effects

: appetite suppression (the dose can be taken after a meal), insomnia, higher HR and BP Other common adverse effects of stimulantsHeadache and stomachache: also commonHeart rate: up 5-10 beats/min on averageSystolic BP: up 4-6 mm Hg on average

Growth in height slows over 2 years of use; adult height may be lower

Tics: can emerge on a stimulant; tics do not rule out a stimulant

New psychotic or manic symptoms: on stimulants Other stimulant warningsSudden death: reported with structural heart diseasePeripheral vasculopathy, including Raynaud phenomenon Watch the fingers and toes

Diagnosed bipolar disorder: small risk of switching to mania

Misuse and diversion: high abuse potential; family members prescribed stimulants are one route to misuse Prescribed stimulant usePrescribed, supervised stimulant: tolerance and withdrawal alone do not make a stimulant use disorder

: nausea, sedation, irritability Atomoxetine contraindicationsNarrow-angle glaucomaPheochromocytoma, present or pastSevere heart or vessel disease that a rise in BP or HR would worsen

Atomoxetine: rare liver injury

Atomoxetine: suicidal ideation in children and teens (boxed warning)

Alpha-2 agonists: , low BP, slow pulse, fainting on standing (orthostatic syncope) Sleepiness with other depressantsOther central nervous system depressants add to the sleepiness

Alpha-2 agonists: rebound hypertension after an abrupt stop

Mania on a stimulantAn episodic course fits bipolar disorder better than chronic ADHD

Dilated pupils (mydriasis) and a fast pulse: stimulant intoxication

If a manic episode begins on a stimulant, choose tapering or stopping the stimulant and treating the mania first.

Atomoxetine liver injuryItching, dark urine, jaundice or right upper quadrant tenderness on atomoxetine, with raised liver enzymes

If jaundice or laboratory evidence of liver injury appears, choose stopping atomoxetine and never restarting it.

Alpha-2 reboundHeadache, agitation, tremor, then a sharp rise in BP and pulse after guanfacine or clonidine is stopped suddenly or doses are missed Worst caseReboundHypertensive encephalopathy has followed an abrupt stop.

Doses often missed favor another drug

If guanfacine or clonidine is to be stopped, choose a slow taper, with BP and HR checked at each step.

DrugEffectManagement

Practice
  1. 9-year-old boy with ADHD; his parents agree to start a stimulant inattention and impulsivity at home and school for 2 years his uncle died suddenly while running at age 28 HR 88/min · BP 104/66 mm Hg · normal heart sounds → Electrocardiogram → sudden cardiac death in the family is a reason to consider an ECG before a stimulant, even with a normal exam
  2. 4-year-old boy brought by his mother for his behavior at home runs off in stores, climbs furniture, interrupts constantly same reports from his preschool teacher for 8 months no injuries; development otherwise normal → Parent training in behavior management → under age 6, behavioral therapy (parent training) comes first; medication is considered if the response is inadequate or symptoms are moderate to severe
  3. 16-year-old boy with ADHD returns after his methylphenidate ran out early his mother found classmates paying him for pills grades slipping; symptoms clearly impair him HR 76/min · BP 118/72 mm Hg → Atomoxetine → a diverted stimulant calls for a nonstimulant: atomoxetine has no addiction risk
  4. 34-year-old woman with ADHD and depression asks to start an ADHD drug stopped phenelzine, taken for depression, 5 days ago takes no other medications HR 72/min · BP 116/74 mm Hg → Wait until 14 days after the last phenelzine dose → stimulants and atomoxetine are contraindicated within 14 days of stopping an MAOI (monoamine oxidase inhibitor)
  5. 11-year-old girl on atomoxetine for 3 months for ADHD 4 days of itching, dark urine and fatigue yellow sclerae; tender right upper quadrant ALT 640 U/L · AST 520 U/L · T 37.0 °C → Stop atomoxetine and do not restart it → jaundice or laboratory evidence of liver injury on atomoxetine: stop it and never restart
  6. 12-year-old boy with ADHD has a headache and feels jittery took guanfacine every day for a year; ran out 3 days ago no stimulant; no new drugs BP 148/96 mm Hg · HR 112/min · pupils normal → Rebound hypertension from stopping guanfacine → guanfacine stopped abruptly brings rebound hypertension and a fast pulse; it is tapered instead
  7. 15-year-old girl with ADHD, on amphetamine for 2 years 6 days of sleeping 2 hours a night without fatigue talks rapidly; plans to start three businesses urine drug screen positive for amphetamine only · HR 90/min → Stop the amphetamine and treat the mania → a distinct episode with little need for sleep is mania, not ADHD; the stimulant is tapered or stopped and the mania treated first
